scenario.speaker: dana
scenario.briefing:
This is it. Twelve weeks ago Neo Smart Living was a name on an RFP; today every piece of evidence we promised them is in the building. The secondary research, the focus groups, the survey — n = 600, coded, cross-tabbed, and clean.

What's left is the part clients actually pay for: **the final report**. Neo's leadership meets next week to decide how to position, feature, and price the Tahoe Mini, and our report is the document that decision rests on.

I'm asking you to assemble it. Profile the respondents honestly — limitations included. Choose visuals that make the findings legible to executives. Run the segment cross-tab Neo asked about. Then take a position: which concepts lead, which product emphases we recommend, and what the price should be.

Marcus has sent you the survey topline; the condensed focus-group findings and the open-end theme counts are in Resources. Everything you need is in the evidence.

I'll be reviewing this one personally. You've earned that — now show me the analyst you've become.

— Dana

inbox.subject: What a final report owes a client
inbox.body:
Before you start assembling, three principles I hold every Summit Point report to:

1. **Findings are not recommendations.** A finding is what the data says ("59.7% named total cost the greatest barrier"). A recommendation is what the client should do about it. Keep them in separate sections, and never let a recommendation appear that you cannot trace to a finding. Executives can smell an unsupported opinion from across the room.

2. **Be honest about limitations.** Every achieved sample differs from the target population somewhere. Our job is to say *where*, and whether the gap could bias a conclusion. But precision matters in both directions: calling a healthy sample characteristic a "limitation" is as sloppy as hiding a real one. Compare the profile against Neo's target definition and call each gap what it is.

3. **Report the inconvenient numbers.** If a result complicates the story — report it, with context. A client who later discovers we buried a number never trusts us again. A client who sees us surface it trusts us forever.

Neo is deciding positioning, features, and price off this document. Work backward from those three decisions, and make every page earn its place.

— Dana

inbox.subject: Survey topline attached — everything is in here
inbox.body:
The full topline from the Neo survey is attached — demographics, barriers, value drivers, the concept test, price expectations, and the segment cuts Dana promised Neo's team. I've checked every number twice against the data file.

My one tip for report week: keep the topline open in a second window the whole time. Every claim in the report should point at a number in this document, and every number you cite should match it to the decimal. If you catch yourself writing a sentence you can't footnote — stop and find the evidence, or cut the sentence.

Good luck. It's been fun watching you get here.

— Marcus

attachments.title: Survey topline results (n = 600)
attachments.body:
**Neo Smart Living — Tahoe Mini Survey Topline (n = 600)**

Fielded online to owner-occupied single-family homeowners in Southern California; 600 completed interviews against the county-stratified sampling plan.

**Respondent profile.** Gender: 51.0% female, 49.0% male. Age: median 58.5 (mean 56.6); 11.7% under 40, 44.0% aged 40–60, 44.3% over 60. Household income: $0–24.9K 11.0% · $25–49.9K 20.5% · $50–74.9K 24.2% · $75–99.9K 16.7% · $100–199.9K 22.0% · $200K+ 5.7% (44.4% at $75K or more). HOA membership: 21.3% yes, 75.0% no, 3.7% not sure. Outdoor recreation: 30.8% never, 29.2% a few times a year, 12.5% about once a month, 12.5% 2–3 times per month, 15.0% weekly or more (40.0% monthly or more).

**Category familiarity.** 27.0% have actively researched or priced a backyard unit; 33.7% have thought about it but not researched; 18.7% are aware but never seriously considered; 20.7% never considered it — so **60.7% have at least thought about the category**. Category interest mean 3.18 (1–5). Purchase interest at the current $23,000 price: 2.34. Likelihood of purchasing within 24 months: 2.05.

**Barriers.** Greatest barrier (single choice): **total cost (~$23,000) 59.7%**; none 7.2%; build quality 6.8%; other 6.0%; HOA rules 5.8%; space/access 4.7%; financing 4.5%; permit uncertainty 3.2%; resale value 2.2%. Concern-battery means (reduces likelihood, 1–5): cost 3.86 · build quality 3.36 · financing 3.17 · resale 3.02 · permit 2.83 · HOA 2.71 · space 2.43.

**Value drivers** (increases likelihood, 1–5): build-quality assurance 3.62 · one-day install speed 3.51 · permit-light design 3.06.

**Concept test** (appeal means, 1–5): Wellness/Studio 3.20 · Simplicity 3.15 · Home Office 3.11 · Guest Suite/Income 2.83 · Adventure 2.77. Single best-concept vote: none of the above 24.0% · Wellness 21.2% · Home Office 19.3% · Guest/Income 13.2% · Simplicity 11.5% · Adventure 10.8%. Stated primary use: storage 26.7% · home office 18.0% · wellness studio 14.8%.

**Price expectations** (medians): too cheap $5,000 · a bargain $8,000 · getting expensive $12,000 · **too expensive $20,000**. Current delivered-and-installed price: $23,000.

**Segment cuts.** Outdoor-active (monthly+ recreation, n = 240) vs. all respondents (n = 600): category interest 3.58 vs 3.18 · purchase interest at $23K 2.80 vs 2.34 · 24-month likelihood 2.42 vs 2.05 · concept appeal: Home Office 3.47 vs 3.11, Wellness 3.53 vs 3.20, Adventure 3.23 vs 2.77 · value drivers: build quality 3.87 vs 3.62, install speed 3.72 vs 3.51 · concerns: cost 3.63 vs 3.86, financing 3.02 vs 3.17. Additional cuts on file: income $100K+ (n = 166) vs under $100K (n = 434); HOA yes (n = 128) vs no (n = 450).

Purchase-likelihood ladder (0–100% stated likelihood): mean likelihood declines steadily across the three fielded price points — $18,000 → $23,000 → $28,000 — with the steepest drop above $23,000.

pages.intro: The report opens with who we actually surveyed. For each result below, choose the interpretation that belongs in the report — compare the achieved sample against Neo's target market (homeowners aged 30–65, household income $75K+) and call each gap, or non-gap, what it is.

tasks.title: Respondent Profile & Limitations
tasks.prompt: For each survey result, select the interpretation that should appear in the report's sample-profile and limitations section. A limitation is a mismatch with Neo's target market that could bias a conclusion — not every imperfection, and not every difference.

options.text: The sample is effectively gender-balanced (51.0% female / 49.0% male), mirroring the homeowner population — report it as evidence of a healthy sample, not as a limitation.
The 2-point female skew over-represents women; flag gender as a sample limitation and recommend weighting the data before any findings are reported.

With a median age of 58.5 and 44.3% of respondents over 60, the sample skews older than Neo's 30–65 target — report it as a limitation and read age-sensitive findings (remote work, adventure uses) with caution.
Older adults are more likely to own homes anyway, so the 58.5 median age simply reflects the market — no age caveat is needed in the report.

Only 44.4% of respondents meet Neo's $75K+ income target — the sample under-represents the target income band. Report it as a limitation: stated purchase interest at $23,000 is likely deflated relative to Neo's actual prospects.
The six income bands cover the full range of households, so the distribution is representative enough as it stands — no income caveat is needed.
At 21.3% yes, HOA membership is consistent with regional HOA prevalence, and the base (n = 128) is large enough to support the HOA segment cuts — not a limitation.
Only 21.3% of respondents belong to an HOA, so HOA members are badly under-represented — flag it as a limitation and drop the HOA cuts from the report.

groups.label: Outdoor recreation frequency
groups.context: Outdoor recreation: **Never 30.8%** · A few times a year 29.2% · Monthly or more 40.0%.

options.text: The distribution is fine for describing the population, but with 30.8% who never recreate outdoors, the overall read on the Adventure concept comes partly from people outside its audience — caveat the overall Adventure numbers and lean on the outdoor-active segment cut.
With 30.8% answering 'never,' the sample is too sedentary to be usable — exclude non-outdoor respondents from all analyses before writing the report.

groups.label: Prior consideration of a backyard unit
groups.context: Actively researched or priced: 27.0% · Thought about it: 33.7% · Aware but not considered: 18.7% · Never considered: 20.7%. **60.7% have at least thought about it.**

options.text: With 60.7% having at least thought about a backyard unit — and 27.0% having actively researched or priced one — category awareness is real. This supports the demand narrative and belongs early in the findings.
Because 60.7% had already considered the category, the sample is biased toward intenders — the report should discount all interest measures as inflated.

groups.label: Greatest barrier (single choice)
groups.context: **Total cost (~$23,000): 59.7%** · none 7.2% · build quality 6.8% · other 6.0% · HOA rules 5.8% · space 4.7% · financing 4.5% · permit 3.2% · resale 2.2%.

options.text: Cost at 59.7% is the decisive finding of the study — nearly nine times the runner-up. It must lead the findings section and drive the pricing recommendation.
Cost always tops barrier questions, so the 59.7% is mostly a survey artifact — mention it briefly and give the other barriers roughly equal billing.

groups.label: Best-concept vote: 'none of the above'
groups.context: Best-concept vote: **none of the above 24.0%** · Wellness/Studio 21.2% · Home Office 19.3% · Guest/Income 13.2% · Simplicity 11.5% · Adventure 10.8%.

options.text: 'None of the above' at 24.0% is the single most-chosen response — report it honestly as a cautionary statistic: even the best positioning leaves roughly a quarter of homeowners unmoved.
The 24.0% 'none' vote muddies the story — exclude those respondents and re-percentage the concept votes so the winners read more decisively.

resources.title: Focus-group findings — condensed summary (Round 7)
resources.body: **Neo Smart Living focus groups — condensed findings.** Across the sessions, homeowners responded warmly to the idea of a bright, finished, multi-use backyard room — with wellness/exercise and home-office uses volunteered most often and discussed most concretely. The one-day installation drew genuine surprise and approval. Climate control was treated as a gate to year-round use: participants repeatedly asked about summer heat and insulation. The floor-to-ceiling glass, shown in concept images, drew consistent **privacy and heat** objections — several participants asked for privacy panels or reduced glazing on neighbor-facing sides. The smart entry lock earned shrugs; nobody named it as a reason to buy. On price, participants who knew the category anchored on real competitors' advertised prices — the Autonomous WorkPod's $20,900 was the reference — and set their expectations **below** them for an unproven brand. The written price-ladder medians landed at **$9,000 (bargain), $13,000 (getting expensive), and $19,000 (too expensive to consider)** for a delivered-and-installed unit — a ceiling under the Tahoe Mini's current $23,000.

guides.title: Round 12 — From Findings to Recommendations
guides.body:
**The anatomy of a research report.** Objectives → method → sample profile & limitations → findings → recommendations. Each section has one job, and the discipline is keeping them apart:

- A **finding** is what the data says. A **recommendation** is what the client should do. Never present the second without tracing it to the first — and never dress an opinion up as a finding.
- **Limitations are comparisons, not confessions.** Set the achieved sample next to the target-population definition. A *limitation* is a mismatch that could bias a conclusion the client will act on. A characteristic that matches the population — or that simply looks imperfect but biases nothing — is not a limitation, and calling it one erodes the client's trust in the caveats that matter.
- **Report the inconvenient numbers.** Excluding or re-percentaging results to make a story cleaner is the fastest way to lose a client permanently. Surface the awkward statistic yourself and give it honest context.

**For this round:** Neo's target is homeowners aged 30–65 with household income $75K+. Judge each profile result against that definition — some achieved characteristics match it, some genuinely don't. And when a segment shows a stronger read than the total sample, that's not a flaw to apologize for; it's a targeting insight to report.

guides.title: Round 12 — Choosing the Right Chart
guides.body:
**Match the chart to the data relationship, not to taste.**

| The reader must see… | Use |
|---|---|
| A **comparison** across categories (means, counts) | Bar / column chart — sort by value when categories have no natural order |
| A **composition** (parts of one whole, sums to 100%) | Pie/donut (few slices) or a sorted bar, which compares shares more precisely |
| A **trend** over an ordered dimension (time, price) | Line chart |
| A **distribution** across ordered bins | Histogram / column chart in bin order — never resort ordered bins |
| A **segment comparison** within categories | Grouped (clustered) bar chart |

**Label integrity rules:**

- Means on a rating scale are *not* parts of a whole — never pie them.
- Ordered categories (income bands, price points) keep their natural order; alphabetizing destroys the shape.
- No 3-D effects — they distort every comparison they touch.
- Bar axes start at zero; sort nominal categories largest-first so the ranking reads instantly.
- If a chart needs a paragraph to explain, the form is wrong — and raw quotes are illustration, not analysis: count the themes first, then chart the counts.

guides.title: Round 12 — Reading a Cross Tabulation
guides.body:
**A cross-tab sets a segment's result next to the total sample's.** The working rule: compare the segment mean to the overall mean. A segment mean **at or above** the overall mean says the segment over-indexes on that item; below says it under-indexes.

Three habits keep cross-tab reading honest:

1. **Check the base size first.** A segment of n = 240 supports mean comparisons comfortably; a segment of n = 30 does not. Report the n with every cut.
2. **Mind what the scale means.** On an interest or appeal item, a higher segment mean is *more* favorable. On a concern or barrier item, a higher mean means *more* blocked — so a segment sitting below the overall mean on a barrier is *less* deterred, which can be exactly the story.
3. **Look for the pattern, not the row.** One elevated row is a curiosity; the same segment elevated across interest, appeal, and drivers — while sitting lower on barriers — is a targeting insight worth a page of the report.

guides.title: The House Reporting Standard
guides.body:
Summit Point deliverables follow one written standard - the same rules your report tasks are scored against, stated once:

- **Charts carry percents, not raw counts** - counts depend on base sizes the reader doesn't hold in mind; percents compare.
- **No pie charts.** If shares must be shown, a sorted bar does it more legibly - nine categories with one at 59.7% turn slices into slivers.
- **Every chart sits with its finding** - same page or facing page, labeled axes, a title that states the takeaway rather than the variable name.
- **One short heading per research question** (five words or fewer), with the full research question stated beneath it, findings in the same order the questions were posed.
- **At least one differences question is tested formally**, with the statistics footnoted (test, statistic, df, p) - not narrated vaguely.
- **Limitations are mismatches that could bias a conclusion** - named specifically, with numbers - not a list of everything imperfect and not an apology.
- **Recommendations trace to findings**, each with its rationale and an honest trust boundary: act on this now; validate that before betting on it.
- **Third person, past tense** for what was done and found; the questionnaire and the question-to-item map ride in the appendix so any number can be traced to its source.

Round pointer: every task in this round is one of these rules in miniature. Score high here and the written report is mostly assembled.
